title: Cancer data at scale
summary: TCGA, PCAWG, cBioPortal, DepMap, GDSC and OncoKB; controlled access; FAIR data; and the shape of omics data — many features, few patients, batch effects.

shots.title:
Cancer data,
at scale.
shots.subtitle: What exists, how to get it, and its shape.
shots.narration: Any computational paper in oncology lives or dies on its data. Here is what exists publicly, how access works, and the statistical shape of the data — which matters a great deal for small quantum models.

shots.label: tumours from 33 cancer types in TCGA's PanCancer Atlas
shots.context: DNA, RNA, methylation, microRNA and protein data
shots.narration: The Cancer Genome Atlas profiled about ten thousand tumours from thirty-three cancer types, at many molecular layers.

shots.text: Its molecular clusters were dominated by **cell of origin** — tissue type. Your classifier may be learning the tissue, not the disease.
shots.narration: A striking result: when those tumours were clustered on their molecular data, the clusters were dominated by the tissue the cancer came from. A classifier can easily learn tissue of origin instead of the biology you care about.

shots.label: whole cancer genomes with matched normal tissue (PCAWG)
shots.narration: The Pan-Cancer Analysis of Whole Genomes added two thousand six hundred and fifty-eight whole cancer genomes, with matched normal tissue, across thirty-eight tumour types.

shots.heading: Tools you will use
items: **cBioPortal** — browse mutations and outcomes across studies
**DepMap** — which genes cancer cell lines depend on
**GDSC** — drug sensitivity of cancer cell lines
shots.narration: Four tools you will use constantly: cBioPortal to browse genomic studies; DepMap for which genes cancer cell lines depend on; GDSC for how cell lines respond to drugs; and OncoKB or ESCAT for which alterations are actionable.

shots.text: DepMap: **501** genome-scale screens; in **82%** of predictive models the top biomarkers were **gene-expression** features.
shots.narration: DepMap's first map analysed five hundred and one genome-scale knockdown screens. In eighty-two percent of its predictive models, the best biomarkers were gene-expression features, not mutations.

shots.text: Open data are a click away; **controlled** data need dbGaP authorisation and an eRA Commons login.
shots.narration: Summary data are open. Individual-level genomic data are controlled: in NCI's Genomic Data Commons you need authorisation through dbGaP and an eRA Commons login, granted per project. Plan for this months ahead.

shots.text: Share what you make **FAIR**: findable, accessible, interoperable, reusable — by machines too.
shots.narration: And share what you produce following the FAIR principles: findable, accessible, interoperable and reusable — by machines as well as people.

shots.text: Omics data are **wide**: thousands of features, tens or hundreds of patients. Some features will separate any two groups **by chance**.
shots.narration: Now the shape. Omics data are wide: thousands of features on tens or hundreds of patients. With that many features, some will separate any two groups by pure chance. The next lesson shows how that fools people.

shots.text: **Batch effects** — lab, reagent lot, operator — become disasters when they line up with the outcome.
shots.narration: And measurements carry batch effects from the laboratory, the reagent lot or the operator. They become disasters when they line up with the outcome you are predicting.

shots.text: Small quantum models force **dimension reduction** first — and that step can carry most of the signal.
shots.narration: For quantum models with tens of qubits, everything starts with dimension reduction. In one study, multi-omics data were cut to forty-four principal components to fit the device — so ask how much of the result came from that step.

steps.title: Which resource?
steps.brief: Match each research task to the resource you would start with.

cards.text: Download tumour sequencing reads for a lung cancer cohort (with authorisation)
cards.why: Individual-level data are controlled in the Genomic Data Commons.

cards.text: Which genes do KRAS-mutant cell lines depend on?
cards.why: Genome-scale loss-of-function screens across cancer cell lines.

cards.text: How sensitive are ~700 cell lines to a given anticancer drug?
cards.why: Drug-sensitivity data for 138 drugs in its 2013 release.

cards.text: Quickly check how often TP53 is mutated across published studies
cards.why: An open portal for exploring cancer genomics studies.

cards.text: Is this alteration a validated target with an approved drug?
cards.why: Curated actionability levels and evidence tiers.

questions.prompt: How many cancer types are in TCGA's PanCancer Atlas?
What dominated molecular clustering of the TCGA tumours?
questions.explain: Clusters were organised largely by histology and tissue — a confounder to watch in any pan-cancer model.

questions.prompt: To download individual-level controlled data from the GDC you need…
options: dbGaP authorisation and an eRA Commons login
questions.explain: Permissions are set per project according to dbGaP authorisations.

questions.prompt: When is a batch effect most dangerous?
options: When it is correlated with the outcome
When samples were run on the same day
questions.explain: If cases and controls were processed in different batches, a model can learn the batch.

steps.title: Homework 8 · Get your hands on data

fields.label: 1. On cBioPortal, open one TCGA PanCancer study. Record: number of samples, data types available, the five most frequently mutated genes, and the date you checked.
2. Write a one-paragraph data-access plan for a study using individual-level TCGA RNA-seq: what is open, what is controlled, who must apply, and how long you would budget.
3. Name two confounders (e.g. tissue of origin, batch) that could make a pan-cancer classifier look better than it is, and how you would control each.
